Photograph: Mark Waugh/Alamy Schools Most English secondary schools are breaking healthy food rules, finds report ‘Shocking’ breaches such as sweets and crisps at breakfast uncovered just before expansion of free school meals Denis Campbell Health policy editor Mon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 00.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three-quarters of secondary schools in England are breaking the rules on food offered to pupils by serving chips, burgers and hash browns too often – and sweets and crisps at breakfast time, according to a report. “Shocking” breaches of school food standards have been exposed on Monday, in a new analysis of the food provided at almost 400 state secondaries undertaken by Bite Back, a food charity set up by the chef Jamie Oliver. D’Arcy Williams, Bite Back’s chief executive, said the picture of schools’ widespread noncompliance with the government-set standards that emerged from its analysis was alarming. Three out of four menus it analysed at 391 state secondary schools in England contained at least one breach of the standards. Most involved schools offering unhealthy foods more often than is allowed. At 206 schools (53%), products high in fat, sugar or salt that are meant to be banned altogether – such as crisps, Oreos, Mini Cheddars, chocolate bars and pastries – were being offered to pupils to buy as snacks, including at breakfast time and at lunchtime. Schools are allowed to sell only nuts, seeds, plain vegetables and plain fruit as snacks. The research also found that: There were 224 schools (57%) providing meat products such as burgers, nuggets, sausages and goujons more often than the twice a week permitted by the standards. Hash browns, which as a fried starchy food should be a menu option only twice a week, were being offered more often than that at 144 schools (37%). There were 123 schools (31%) using chocolate in solid form, such as chocolate chips or chocolate coating, as an ingredient in dessert or bakes, despite it being banned. ‘No cheeseburgers … they would go bankrupt’: pupils reject plan to cut fatty foods from lunch menus Read more “These findings are very alarming and expose a system that is fundamentally failing our children,” said Williams. “It is shocking to find crisps and chocolate being pushed at breakfast time or processed meats like sausage rolls and bacon baps being served far more frequently than the rules allow. “Young people have been telling us for years that their school food is ‘beige, bland and boring’ and now we have more evidence that they are being surrounded by unhealthy food throughout the school day. “Schools should be a sanctuary for health and learning, yet the current postcode lottery of food quality is undermining that mission.” But in other findings that parents may find reassuring, only eight schools (2%) were flouting the ban on selling confectionery such as KitKats, Haribo sweets and Maltesers as standalone items. And even fewer – just three schools (1%) – were selling banned sugary drinks such as Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Fanta and Sprite. Campaigners for healthier food voiced concern at the findings. Katharine Jenner, the executive director of the Obesity Health Alliance, said: “Schools should be one of the places where we can be confident children are being given nutritious food. Yet this research suggests too many are still being routinely exposed to processed meat, fried foods, pastries and confectionery beyond what the standards allow. Schools in England must be compelled to offer pupils healthy food, not junk Read more “Children are already growing up surrounded by unhealthy food across the wider food system, from what is marketed to them to what is promoted in shops. If we can’t even get the food environment right in schools, where children spend such a large part of their lives, then we have a serious problem.” Ministers are preparing to unveil an overhaul of the school food standards, which child health and anti-obesity organisations have been seeking for years. At the start of the new academic year in England next month, there will be a major expansion of access to free school meals instigated by the Labour government. From now on, all pupils from a household where someone is receiving universal credit will qualify in England. The Department for Education acknowledged that schools did flout the standards. A spokesperson said: “We want every child to be healthy, happy and ready to learn, and nutritious food plays a vital role in helping them achieve that. “That’s why we are delivering the most ambitious overhaul of school food in a generation, making sure children have access to healthy, balanced meals, get more of their five a day and are protected from the harms of eating too much ultra-processed food. “We know not every school is following these standards, which is exactly why we will introduce a strengthened enforcement regime, alongside requiring every school to publish their food policy and menus online to improve transparency for parents.” Explore more on these topics Schools Food Health Jamie Oliver England Secondary schools news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m3.text: Figure caption, Moment tornado tears through southern France By Yang Tian Published 25 August 2026, 02:27 BST Updated 9 hours ago A tornado has torn through the village of Pomas in south-west France, injuring 39 people and damaging hundreds of homes. Authorities said 15 people were taken to hospital and two were in a critical condition. One man said his pregnant wife was injured after their house collapsed on her. More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the village south of Carcassonne after winds reaching 117km/h (73mph) tore roofs off houses and damaged an estimated 300 homes on Monday. "Half the village has been destroyed," said one resident called Pierre, who described the tornado as swirling like a "huge red and yellow chimney". "There's a huge castle and a third of it is has collapsed - even though these are stones that have stood for 1,000 years," Pierre told Ici Occitanie. Image source, AFP via Getty Images The third stage of the Vuelta a EspaÃ±a cycle race, which was taking place in the Aude area of south-western France, had to be cancelled when a hail storm forced the riders to take shelter about 15km from the finish line. The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials. Local sub-prefect Emmanuelle Plantier-Lemarchand told French radio that she was not aware of anyone missing. She lowered the number of victims from 41 to 39, and said 15 of them had been treated in hospital. "I heard this massive noise... then I saw everything flying around in the air and my roof collapsed over my head," shocked resident Chantal told French radio. "I've got no house left, that's for sure... I was really scared. I thought that's it, this my final hour." Image source, Tim de Waele/Getty Images Image caption, Cyclists in the Vuelta a EspaÃ±a race had to seek shelter in a hotel when they were hit by a hailstorm French authorities had issued an orange alert for thunderstorms in large parts of the country's south-west, which have already been hit by power outages and transport disruptions. Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees. Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Three hundred homes were damaged by the tornado in Pomas Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot. On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service MÃ©tÃ©o-France. It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two. Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Frank Furedi said the thinktank’s failure to provide funds meant it had effectively ceased operations. Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock Thinktanks Head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wages Frank Furedi announces resignation from MCC Brussels after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’ Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.01 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite Brussels thinktank has quit, citing unpaid wages since the change of government in Hungary. The sociology professor Frank Furedi said he was resigning as the executive director of MCC Brussels with “immediate effect” on Monday over “persistent failure to provide the contractually agreed funds”. ‘Attack on civil society’: why Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank is in crisis Read more A spokesperson for MCC Brussels confirmed Furedi’s resignation and said no one working for the organisation in the EU capital had been paid in July or August. MCC Brussels launched in late 2022 with a self-styled mission to shake up political debate in the EU capital, although critics said it defended Orbán’s illiberal rule in Hungary while using a well-funded position to attack civil society groups. It was an ostensibly independent offshoot of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium Foundation in Budapest, a training ground for Orbán’s Fidesz party that was lavishly funded by his rightwing nationalist government. The future of MCC Brussels was thrown into doubt when Péter Magyar won a landslide election victory in April pledging to crack down on corruption in Hungary, which numerous independent organisations said had proliferated during Orbán’s 16 years in power. Soon after his victory, Magyar promised to end state financing for MCC Budapest and to investigate a large transfer of state assets to the organisation, which he described as a crime. Furedi has previously dismissed Magyar’s claims of a criminal transfer of assets to MCC Budapest as “bullshit”, while MCC Brussels said it condemned corruption by all politicians. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace | Editorial Read more In a letter to the senior leadership of MCC Budapest seen by the Guardian, Furedi wrote: “Without the contractually agreed resources, our colleagues cannot function and are facing serious economic hardship. We have been placed in a situation where our individual reputations and the integrity of our intellectual mission are systematically undermined.” The failure to provide funds, Furedi said, meant MCC Brussels had effectively ceased operations and was unable to pay suppliers or meet conditions under Belgian insolvency law. Furedi said he intended to ensure, “along with like-minded individuals, the work and intellectual legacy of our institution will continue to flourish in another form”, without elaborating on future plans. The letter was first reported by Politico . MCC Budapest did not immediately respond to a request for comment. MCC Budapest has also seen change at the top following the election of the new government. The MCC board was previously led by Viktor Orbán’s chief of staff, Balázs Orbán, who is no relation to the former prime minister. Balázs Orbán, now an MP for the Fidesz party, announced he was standing down as chair in June. The MCC Brussels spokesperson said after Furedi’s resignation and a round of lay-offs in June and July, MCC Brussels was down to 12 staff and three research fellows. Before the cuts it had employed 25 people and was one of the best-funded thinktanks in Brussels. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text: US politics live with Shrai Popat US news Donald Trump claims ‘Iran war will end very soon’ as midterm rallies heat up – US politics live The US president said that the war will end ‘as soon as I want it to end’ as the midterms take place under a cloud of economic uncertainty Sign up for the Breaking News US email to get newsletter alerts in your inbox Siraj Datoo Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.26 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.27 EDT Share Key events 21m ago Donald Trump claims Iran war 'will end very soon' US President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen US President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images Siraj Datoo Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.26 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.27 EDT Share From 21m ago US president Donald Trump claimed the Iran war ‘will end very soon,’ as voters consider their options ahead of midterm elections that are taking place amid economic uncertainty and ongoing global conflict. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday evening, Trump said : “The Iran war will end very soon. It’s going to end very soon, as soon as I want it to end, it’ll end.” He added that Iran would “never have a nuclear weapon” and that oil prices would “drop like a rock”. The US president has in recent weeks attempted to shift focus towards Ukraine, and has suggested that its attack on Russian refineries are responsible for rising fuel prices. His renewed messaging on Iran suggests that the price of daily goods – and gas at the tank – are having an impact at the polls. Voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms are increasingly disenchanted with the economy , according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession. Elsewhere: James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, faced a grilling from undecided voters on a range of issues from Gaza to his faith at a town hall. Something he emphasized was his aspiration to put residents above party allegiance. Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt ‘betrayed’ by the US after Ukraine’s military access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite was restricted. The US president has denied that the administration has cut intelligence sharing but Musk suggested on X that the US government was behind the restrictions . Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing scrutiny over her claims that she’s a lawyer. Zacharia has clarified some of the questions but the big one remains: has she ever passed the bar?
